title: Seriatim throttling experiments - field notes
body:
Context:
- Running a set of short-lived clients (mobile/web) that send small prompts (~30-60 tokens).
- Observed pathological tail latencies when a single tenant connection submits serial requests: head-of-line (HoL) from long-running requests blocks short ones.
- Coined working term: "seriatim" pattern = many small requests arriving in strict sequence (one after another) from the same connection/tenant, exacerbating HoL.

Goal:
- Understand how different throttling/smoothing heuristics affect p50/p95/p99 and sustained qps under seriatim arrivals.
- Find lightweight mitigation that doesn't require major runtime refactor.

Env and harness:
- Serving runtime: local cluster (4x A10G-like), dockerized microbench harness.
- Model: open Llama-2-7B trimmed to 8-bit. KV cache warm when noted.
- Client: synthetic generator that can emit patterns: seriatim, poisson, bursty. Ran seriatim walks of 1k requests per run.
- Metrics captured: request lat, token lat, queue depth, latency percentiles, throughput (req/s), model utilization.

Baseline (no smoothing, default scheduler) - run A (cold-KV, seriatim):
- concurrency: ~1.0 per connection (by design)
- p50: 85ms, p95: 420ms, p99: 1.8s
- sustained qps: 18 r/s (across the node pool)
- notes: clear long tail; a handful of requests incur >1s due to small internal preemption and cache warm episodes when earlier requests produced long generation windows.

Run B - tiny fixed micro-delay between serial requests (client paced 8ms gap):
- rationale: reduce immediate back-to-back enqueueing spikes; gives runtime loop a chance to coalesce with other tenants/requests.
- p50: 74ms, p95: 370ms, p99: 1.25s
- qps: 16.7 r/s (slight drop)
- notes: tail improved moderately, but still heavy p99s. Client-side delay is cheap but shifts load -> slightly lower qps.

Run C - server-side windowed smoothing (per-connection token-budget window):
- heuristic: allow X tokens per 100ms per-connection; if exceeded, apply soft backpressure with 5-50ms jittered hold.
- config used: X=150 tokens/100ms, hold jitter uniform(5,25)ms.
- p50: 70ms, p95: 310ms, p99: 840ms
- qps: 17.2 r/s
- notes: significant p99 improvement w/o large qps hit. Jitter avoids synchronization artifacts. Implementation was a small middleware shim (proof-of-concept).

Run D - per-tenant FIFO weight + opportunistic reordering:
- heuristic: within a tenant, allow short requests (<120ms expected) to jump ahead of long-running ones if they won't cause model-context corruption; (best-effort).
- safety: only allowed when generation hasn't started or when the request is below token threshold.
- p50: 68ms, p95: 295ms, p99: 760ms
- qps: 17.4 r/s
- notes: nice for mixed-length workloads; complexity increases and requires careful invariants. Cleanest when combined with cache-tagging metadata.

Run E - adaptive throttling based on rolling P95 windows per-connection:
- heuristic: if connection p95 > target (500ms), reduce per-connection admission rate by 20%, otherwise slowly ramp up.
- p50: 72ms, p95: 280ms, p99: 700ms
- qps: 16.9 r/s
- notes: adapts well but chasing metric can oscillate if window too small. We used smoothing window=30s.

Micro-observations (raw snippets):
- Frequent pattern: sequence A (small req) then B (long req) — when B enters model generation, A is queued with no preemption -> A waits full gen time.
- ASCII timeline (simplified):
  client:   A   B   C   D
  server:   [A___waiting][B=======GEN][C_wait][D_wait]
  where B's GEN blocks others.

Quick ASCII histogram (p99 delta across runs):
- baseline: 1800ms |======
- micro-delay: 1250ms |====
- windowed-smooth: 840ms |===
- reorder: 760ms |===
- adaptive: 700ms |===

Conclusions / heuristics we like:
1) Windowed per-connection token smoothing (Run C) gives the best tradeoff for seriatim arrivals: modest implementation effort + big tail win.
2) Opportunistic short-request reordering (Run D) is powerful for mixed-length sessions but needs safety checks and data tagging.
3) Client pacing (Run B) helps but is not a reliable fix: you must control many clients to apply globally.
4) Adaptive admission (Run E) stabilizes overloaded tenants but needs good damping (avoid 1s windows).

Implementation notes (for a follow PR):
- Create middleware layer: per-connection token-window counter + jittered hold. Keep the state in connection struct; eviction TTL=2m.
- Expose smoothing config via route metadata (so enterprise customers can tune).
- Add lightweight metric 'seriatim-index' = fraction of requests with inter-arrival < 10ms; useful as knob.

Open questions / follow ups:
- How does this interact with dedicated/Dedicated-pools where tenant isolation is stronger? Might still be beneficial for per-connection microbursts.
- Edge cases: server push/streaming requests — smoothing must not introduce perceived streaming lag. Need to bypass for streaming APIs unless token-budget mode integrated with streaming chunking.
- Cost: does smoothing increase total model time (due to less perfect batching)? Early runs show <5% model-util loss; acceptable for SLO improvements.

Next experiments I'd run:
- Combine windowed smoothing + short-request opportunistic reorder and measure end-to-end user-perceived latency on real client traces.
- Vary token-window sizes (50,100,150 tokens per 100ms) and jitter distributions.
- Run on quantized vs fp16 to measure interaction with generation time variance.

To-do (actionable):
- [ ] Draft PR for middleware shim (owner: Lee) - include config and metrics.
- [ ] Add seriatim-index telemetry (owner: Maya).
- [ ] Run combined heuristic experiment on dedicated pool (owner: Ravi).

Notes to self: keep experiment configs saved under perf/harness/seriatim/<timestamp>.yaml; link in PR for reproducibility. Tag linear ticket PERF-4321 when opening PR.

Misc scribbles:
- possible name for feature: "connection smoothing" or "seriatim-mitigation". Favor "connection smoothing" (less jargony).
- if we expose per-route smoothing, default=off for backward compatibility, but enable as opt-in for new low-latency routes.

End of notes.
